strengths: The paper addresses a clear and relevant gap: existing visual CoT datasets are small, single-step, and 2D-only. VISREASON (489K examples across four domains) plus the 165K depth-informed VISREASON-PRO subset is a substantial scale-up over prior process-supervision resources such as Visual-CoT, with a useful 'zoom-and-verify' structure that could benefit the community.

The depth-aware extension is a meaningful and relatively novel angle: attaching pseudo-3D cues (monocular depth, segmentation-derived object lists with ordinal depths) and generating QA pairs that couple 2D layout with depth relations goes beyond most prior grounded-CoT datasets.

Evidence is reasonably comprehensive: results on the Visual-CoT benchmark, a dedicated RoI-localization and 3D-grounding protocol, external generalization tests (MME, V*), an ablation over dataset components and the adaptive zoom strategy, and a human study covering answer accuracy, grounded faithfulness, and stepwise clarity.

Reproducibility support is above average: the supplementary material provides full training configurations, detailed pseudo-code for both generation pipelines, all evaluation protocols, and every prompt used for data generation, refinement, grounding augmentation, and grading. The paper commits to releasing the dataset and benchmark.

The paper is honest in several places about trade-offs, e.g., acknowledging that Qwen2.5-VL retains an edge on text/doc OCR tasks and that grounded ratios and depth prediction remain difficult for all models.
weaknesses: The contribution type is best classified as Datasets/Benchmarks, not Algorithms/General; the paper does not really state this, and the framing ('unified training and inference pipeline') oversells what is essentially SFT of Qwen2.5-VL with LoRA on generated traces. Under a Datasets/Benchmarks lens the absence of a novel algorithm is fine, but the methodological contribution is thin.

A circularity concern affects the headline VisREASON-PRO benchmark results (Tab. 3 and 4): the benchmark is drawn from the same GQA-derived VISREASON-PRO data on which the model was trained. Evaluating RoI localization and 3D grounding on in-distribution, self-annotated 'ground truth' (final-round CoT boxes, DepthAnything-derived pseudo-depth) favors the trained model by construction, and the single-round baseline comparison is also structurally disadvantaged. Independent held-out evaluation would substantially strengthen these claims.

The '3D grounding' terminology overstates the contribution. The depth signal is monocular pseudo-depth with ordinal ranking, not metric 3D; the depth error metric measures agreement with DepthAnything-V2 predictions rather than physical depth, so 'lower depth error' partially reflects mimicry of the annotation tool rather than genuine spatial understanding.

Annotation quality is machine-generated (GPT-4.1-Nano/Mini) with no reported human verification or inter-annotator statistics for the 489K/165K traces. Quality control is limited to automated 'verify-and-fix' routines; hallucinated rationales or implausible zoom chains could be systematically reinforced through SFT. The 30-rater/20-item user study is too small to substitute for dataset validation.

The dataset is heavily derivative: it builds directly on the Visual-CoT seed images/QA pairs and source datasets (TextVQA, DocVQA, GQA, etc.), with the main novelty being the trace generation and depth augmentation. Attribution is given, but positioning the contribution clearly relative to VisCoT, Chain-of-Focus, and ARGUS deserves more careful differentiation.

There is an apparent inconsistency between the described automatic evaluation protocol (models terminate on their own within Rmax rounds) and the qualitative inference examples (Figs. 20-22), where a human repeatedly intervenes with 'Please think further...'. This makes it unclear how the visualized behavior was produced and how representative it is.

Gains over the strongest baseline (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) are modest in absolute terms (0.807 vs. 0.770 average), and the base model actually beats the proposed models on most Doc/Text subsets. The LLM-judge scoring uses coarse fixed score bands (e.g., 0.85-0.94), which may compress or distort cross-model differences.
No limitations or societal-impact discussion is provided; issues such as bias inherited from source datasets, licensing of derived data, or failure modes of learned zoom behavior are not addressed.

strengths: The paper addresses a real gap: large-scale, multi-round, spatially grounded visual chain-of-thought supervision. The scale (489K examples, 165K richer subset) and breadth across four domains exceed most prior visual-CoT datasets, which the related-work discussion motivates reasonably well.

The data-generation pipeline is described in unusual detail: the supplementary material includes full pseudocode (Algorithms 1-2), all prompts, iterative zoom refinement with GT-coverage adjustment, and a consistency-checking pass. This supports reproducibility of the annotation recipe.

Training details are thorough (LoRA configuration, hardware, hyperparameters in Tables 8-9), and the models show consistent, if moderate, gains over the Qwen2.5-VL-7B backbone, including on external benchmarks (V*) and in a human evaluation with reasonable criteria (AA, GF, SCS).

The ablation study (Table 6) usefully separates contributions of the dataset variants and the adaptive zoom-in strategy, and the benchmark evaluation protocols for RoI localization and 3D grounding are spelled out precisely.
Appropriate attribution is given: the work is explicitly built on the Visual-CoT seed [44] and the GQA portion, and source datasets are cited in Table 1.
weaknesses: The core annotations are synthetic, generated by GPT-4.1-Nano/Mini conditioned on pseudo-depth and segmentation, yet the paper provides no human verification of rationale quality, factual correctness, or hallucination rates in the training data. For a dataset paper whose central claim is 'high-quality, human-like' supervision, the absence of any annotation-quality audit is a substantive shortcoming, not a minor one.

The headline '3D grounding' contribution rests on pseudo-ground-truth derived from monocular depth estimation (Depth-Anything V2) rather than real 3D annotation. Evaluating models by absolute depth error against monocular relative depth is metrically dubious: monocular depth is affine-ambiguous up to scale/shift, so 'absolute error' in [0,1] is not a well-calibrated physical quantity. The paper conflates ordinal ranking with absolute depth prediction (the ground truth is described as 'ordinal depth ranking' but the metric is absolute difference).

The main RoI/detection comparison (Table 3) is acknowledged in the paper itself to be unfair: the authors' models use multi-round zoom-and-verify and take the refined last-round box, while baselines must emit a single-step prediction. Improvements on this benchmark therefore largely measure the inference-time interactive interface rather than the dataset's value, weakening the central evidence that the data (as opposed to the evaluation protocol) is responsible for gains.

Circularity concerns in the VisReason-Pro benchmark: both the ground-truth RoIs and the ground-truth object sets for 3D grounding are produced by the same generator family (GPT-4.1) and pipeline that produce the training data and, in part, the models' expected output format. The metrics partly measure stylistic conformity to the authors' own annotation schema.

The absolute performance improvement over the already-strong Qwen2.5-VL-7B backbone is modest (0.807 vs. 0.770 average), and the models degrade on text/doc OCR tasks relative to the backbone (Table 2), which the paper explains away qualitatively without a focused analysis or fix.

No decontamination discussion: VisReason-Pro is built from the GQA portion of Visual-CoT, and evaluation also includes GQA; the paper should explicitly demonstrate train/test separation for all 11 source test sets given the aggressive data construction on the same sources.

Internal inconsistencies and sloppiness undermine confidence: the main text states learning rates of 2e-5 (LLM/projector) and 2e-6 (ViT encoder), while the supplementary states 1e-5 with the vision tower fully frozen; there are typos in the paper's own flagship examples ('Tabacco Products' in Fig. 1), table captions ('Blod', 'Relatio Reasoning'), and a likely data-quality error in Fig. 18 where a figure described as a 'person in red clothing' answers 'sitting on a seesaw'. For a dataset contribution, errors in showcased examples are particularly damaging.

The human study is small (30 raters, 20 items per method) and provides no inter-rater reliability or significance analysis; given the subjective criteria (faithfulness, clarity), this evidence is weak support for the paper's claims.

The contribution type is best read as Datasets/Benchmarks. Judged under that lens, the marginal novelty over Visual-CoT [44], Chain-of-Focus [67], DualFocus, and V* is incremental: the main additions are scale, GPT-4.1-based rationale expansion, and pseudo-depth cues from off-the-shelf models. Under this framing the lack of human annotation validation and the pseudo-GT benchmark issues weigh more heavily than they would for an algorithms paper.

The 'human-like global-to-local cognition' framing is asserted repeatedly but never operationalized or tested against alternatives (e.g., why multi-round rationales beat single well-chosen crops is not isolated beyond the coarse ablation).

strengths: Large-scale, process-level dataset: VisReason (489K) and VisReason-Pro (165K) provide multi-round visual CoT supervision with RoIs and rationales across four domains, addressing a real gap (limited scale, single-step reasoning, weak depth-awareness) in prior visual-CoT resources.

The depth-informed Pro subset (Depth-Anything V2 + Mask2Former + SAM2 pseudo-3D cues, 2D+depth relational QA generation) is a distinctive contribution relative to existing 2D-only visual CoT datasets.

Comprehensive evaluation: results on Visual-CoT-Benchmark, MME, V*, a dedicated RoI/3D-grounding benchmark, an ablation over dataset components and the adaptive zoom strategy, plus a blinded human study, provide multi-angle evidence.

Reproducibility is well supported: the supplementary material gives full training configurations, data-generation algorithms, all prompts, and evaluation protocols, and the dataset is stated to be released.
The paper is clearly written, with a well-motivated framing (global-to-local 'zoom-and-verify') and consistent claims that are largely matched by the experiments.

Contribution type: this is a Datasets/Benchmarks paper; judged as such, the scale, diversity, annotation format, and released benchmark constitute an appropriately significant contribution without needing a novel algorithm.
weaknesses: Annotation quality is essentially unverified by humans: the entire corpus is generated by GPT-4.1-Nano (VisReason) and GPT-4.1-Mini (Pro). The paper markets the Pro annotator as 'expert-level', but GPT-4.1-Mini is a small model, and no systematic human audit of rationale correctness, hallucination rate, or box quality at scale is reported. The 20-item user study (30 raters) is too small to validate a 489K-example corpus.

Evaluation comparability concerns: on the VISREASON-PRO benchmark, their models are evaluated with multi-round zoom tools and use the refined last-round RoI, whereas baselines give a single-step prediction. Although acknowledged, this design partly conflates dataset quality with the evaluation protocol and evaluation-time advantage.

Potential train/eval overlap: the training data is derived from the Visual-CoT dataset and evaluation follows the Visual-CoT-Benchmark protocol on its source datasets; the paper should more explicitly verify disjointness of images/splits and discuss contamination risk.

Gains over the strong Qwen2.5-VL-7B backbone are mixed: the trained models lose substantially on text/doc tasks in Tab. 2 (e.g., DocVQA 0.964→0.928), and the ablation (Tab. 6) shows adding Pro degrades Doc/Text accuracy (0.920→0.864/0.856), which somewhat undercuts the 'balanced cross-domain' claim.

The 3D grounding evaluation relies on pseudo-GT depths from monocular estimation, so depth metrics measure agreement with noisy proxies rather than true physical depth; the paper does not quantify this noise floor.

Minor issues reduce polish: inconsistent learning rate between main text (2e-5) and Table 8 (1e-5), duplicated references ([67] vs [68]), a truncated sentence in the supplementary ('warmup ratio of 1'), and Fig. 4 statistics are hard to parse.
Interpretability benefits are asserted but only lightly tested; the human study and qualitative figures are suggestive rather than definitive evidence that the CoT traces improve faithfulness.

strengths: Substantial dataset contribution: VisReason (489K) and VisReason-Pro (165K) provide large-scale, multi-round, RoI-grounded visual CoT supervision with depth-informed annotations across four domains, addressing a real gap in process-level (rather than answer-only) multimodal supervision.

The paper is unusually candid in its error analysis: it explicitly quantifies the Doc/Text degradation under multi-round CoT inference, shows direct-QA recovery (Tab. 3/12), reports the near-zero overall gain for the second backbone (InternVL, +0.001 overall; Tab. 13), and characterizes the source-removal ablation as a diagnostic rather than evidence of source-agnostic transfer.

Thorough methodological hygiene: stratified human audit of 2,200 annotations with Wilson 95% CIs, human calibration of the GPT-4o-mini judge (Pearson r=0.758, QWK=0.819), full prompts, algorithms, and hyperparameters in the supplementary material support reproducibility.

Reasonable gains exactly where the supervision is most aligned with the tasks (CUB 0.681→0.831; OpenImages 0.498→0.805), plus a human user study showing improvements in grounded faithfulness and stepwise clarity, and the adaptive 'zoom only when needed' design is a sensible efficiency consideration.

Given the contribution type (Datasets/Benchmarks — the paper is best judged as a dataset/benchmark contribution rather than a novel algorithm), the evidence of annotation quality, scale, and downstream utility is appropriately emphasized and largely adequate.
weaknesses: Limited held-out generalization evidence: the headline evaluation uses the same 11 source datasets (Visual-CoT) that the training data is derived from. The authors' own source-removal ablation (Tab. 14) shows large dependence on domain-matched supervision, so the fine-grained/spatial gains on CUB and OpenImages may largely reflect in-domain specialization rather than transferable reasoning ability.

Potential circularity in the VisReason-Pro claims: depth annotations come from Depth-Anything V2/Mask2Former, the Pro benchmark's '3D grounding' GT is derived from those same pseudo-depth signals, and the depth questions are generated by a VLM conditioned on that object list. Improvements on Tab. 5 may therefore measure mimicry of the annotation pipeline rather than genuine ordinal-depth or spatial understanding; the paper acknowledges pseudo-depth but does not probe this circularity.

The 'ground truth' RoIs in the VisReason-Pro detection suite are model-generated boxes (only constrained to contain the GT box), which weakens the force of the IoU@0.5/@0.75 comparisons in Tab. 4; baselines are also evaluated through a bespoke multi-round zoom interface that may be comparatively unfamiliar to them.

Overall headline improvement is modest (0.770→0.802 weighted average) and partly an artifact of the multi-round output format; Doc/Text and VSR actually degrade under the intended CoT protocol, and the external MME/V* results show clear regression under multi-round inference.

Comparison with the closest contemporary 'thinking with images' methods (e.g., Pixel Reasoner, Chain-of-Focus, CogCoM-style pipelines trained on comparable data budgets) is absent from the main results table, making it hard to gauge VisReason's value relative to RL-based alternatives the paper itself mentions.

Annotation quality is non-uniform: rationale necessity/faithfulness in Text/Doc is only ~71-72%, and the base generator is GPT-4.1-Nano (a relatively weak annotator); the 86.5% overall rationale metrics mean roughly one in seven rationales may be unnecessary or unfaithful, which is a non-trivial noise floor for process-level supervision.
A societal-impact/licensing and data-consent discussion (for the aggregated source datasets and release terms) is missing.

strengths: Scale and coverage: VisReason aggregates 489K examples across four domains (text/doc, fine-grained, general VQA, spatial relations) with multi-round, RoI-grounded rationales, going beyond prior single-step visual-CoT datasets (Visual-CoT, Chain-of-Spot, V*); VisReason-Pro adds pseudo-depth and segmentation cues, which is a somewhat distinctive supervision signal for ordinal-depth reasoning.

Unusually thorough evaluation methodology for a dataset paper: the inference-format mismatch analysis (Tab. 3, Tab. 12), second-backbone transfer (Tab. 6, 13), source-removal ablation (Tab. 14), a 2,200-example human audit with Wilson confidence intervals (Tab. 15), and calibration of the GPT-4o-mini judge against human ratings (Tab. 16) are commendably transparent.

Honest limitations section: the authors explicitly acknowledge cascading localization failures, noisy pseudo-depth (not metric 3D), and the weakness of Text/Doc rationales; the supplementary material releases full prompts, algorithms, and training configs, supporting reproducibility.

Clear and generally well-organized presentation, with a sensible distinction between multi-round CoT inference and direct-QA inference that clarifies where the method helps (fine-grained/spatial) and where it hurts (Doc/Text, external benchmarks).
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the paper is a re-annotation and expansion of the Visual-CoT seed using GPT-4.1-Nano/Mini, following a well-trodden recipe (zoom-and-verify traces as in CogCoM, VoCoT, Chain-of-Focus, Pixel Reasoner, VGR). The core 'global-to-local zoom-and-verify' idea is not new; the delta over Visual-CoT is richer rationales and pseudo-depth cues, which is an incremental dataset contribution.

In-domain evaluation raises contamination/overfitting concerns: the headline gains are measured on the 11 source test sets of the same datasets used for training (e.g., Birds 0.681→0.831, OpenImages 0.498→0.805). These likely reflect domain-matched specialization rather than transferable reasoning gains. On external benchmarks (MME, V*), the model degrades under its own multi-round CoT inference (V*: 0.791→0.603), and the recovery only comes from switching back to the vanilla direct-QA format — i.e., the base model's original behavior, not a new capability.

Circularity in the depth evaluation: the '3D grounding' ground truth (Tab. 5) is derived from Depth-Anything V2 pseudo-depth — the same signal used to construct the supervision — so low depth error (0.266) mostly measures imitation of the annotator model, not genuine spatial/3D understanding. The paper concedes this but the framing of 'depth-augmented spatial reasoning' overstates the evidential value.

Overall quantitative gains are modest and mixed: the weighted average improves from 0.770 to 0.802 largely on two subsets, while several subsets (VSR, GQA for the InternVL backbone) regress; IoU numbers in Tab. 4/5 are low in absolute terms (0.278 IoU, 0.276 grounded ratio), suggesting the localization behavior itself remains weak.

The rationale quality audit itself reveals weak spots (rationale necessity/faithfulness only 86.5% overall, dropping to ~71% for Text/Doc), meaning a non-trivial fraction of the multi-round supervision may be unnecessary or unfaithful rationales that models are nonetheless trained to imitate; the impact of this noise on training is not analyzed.
Inference-cost trade-off of iterative zoom-and-verify is acknowledged but never quantified (no latency, token-count, or compute measurements), despite being a central design choice.

The claimed 'expert-curated' VisReason-Pro is generated by GPT-4.1-Mini with automated verify-and-fix; 'expert-curated' appears to be a misnomer, and the paper does not clarify what human curation (beyond audits) was involved.

strengths: Substantial dataset contribution: VisReason (489K) and VisReason-Pro (165K) provide large-scale, multi-round, RoI-grounded visual chain-of-thought supervision across four domains, extending prior single-step visual CoT datasets (e.g., Visual-CoT) with process-level traces and depth-informed spatial cues.

The pipeline is well specified and reproducible: the supplementary material includes full data-generation algorithms, all prompts, verification-and-fix routines, detailed hyperparameters, and stated plans for release, which is appropriate rigor for a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution.

Evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: comparisons on the Visual-CoT benchmark, a held-out VisReason-Pro suite with RoI and depth-grounding metrics, external benchmarks (MME, V*), a second-backbone transfer (InternVL-2.5-8B), a human user study, a stratified 2,200-example human audit with Wilson confidence intervals, and calibration of the GPT-4o-mini judge against human ratings.

The paper is commendably honest: it openly analyzes the Doc/Text performance drop and attributes it to inference-format mismatch with a controlled direct-QA comparison, discloses the format dependence on external benchmarks (Table 7), identifies cascading localization failures as a mechanistic weakness, and frames the source-removal ablation as diagnostic rather than claiming source-agnostic generalization.

The ablations (dataset variants, adaptive zoom-in strategy) isolate the contributions of richer supervision versus selective zooming, and the depth/ordinal supervision is carefully presented as pseudo-depth rather than metric 3D, avoiding overclaiming.
weaknesses: Synthetic annotation quality is tied to the teacher models (GPT-4.1-Nano/Mini), and the automatic evaluation judge (GPT-4o-mini) shares a family with the annotators, raising potential circularity/favoritism concerns; human calibration helps, but a fully independent evaluation protocol would strengthen the case.

There is a train/test overlap concern: the models are trained on the source datasets (TextVQA, DocVQA, GQA, etc.) and evaluated on test splits of the same sources within the Visual-CoT benchmark; the source-removal ablation itself shows large drops (e.g., GQA 0.340, Open Images 0.250) when domain-relevant sources are removed, indicating the reported gains depend strongly on matched-domain supervision.

Average gains over the already-strong Qwen2.5-VL-7B baseline are modest (0.770 to 0.802), and performance degrades on some tasks (Doc/Text under multi-round CoT, VSR: 0.705 to 0.654); the value proposition rests mostly on fine-grained (CUB) and Open Images gains.

The VisReason-Pro benchmark ground truth (final-round CoT RoIs, ordinal depths) is generated by the same pipeline being evaluated, so the detection/grounding metrics in Tables 4-5 are partly self-referential; the depth error metric is computed against pseudo-depth rather than any independent measurement.

The user study is small (30 raters, 20 items per method), and while the human audit is larger, several qualitative claims (e.g., 'human-like reasoning', 'cornerstone for the next generation of multimodal intelligence') exceed what the evidence establishes.

The core construction recipe (GPT-generated multi-round traces with GT-box-constrained zoom refinement) is conceptually similar to concurrent grounded visual CoT pipelines, so the novelty lies mainly in scale, depth augmentation, and the depth-aware Pro subset rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.
